n0001.title: GPT-3 And The Scaling Hypothesis
n0001.gist: GPT-3's meta-learning and unbroken scaling curves show that simply making neural nets larger yields qualitatively new abilities, supporting the scaling hypothesis that scale is the secret of AGI.

n0002.title: GPT-3: Meta-Learning, Scaling, Implications
n0002.gist: GPT-3 surprised by learning to learn from examples, implying that scale brings blessings, that the scaling hypothesis may be the path to AGI, and that AI researchers' forecasts lack any coherent model.

n0005.title: Meta-Learning
n0005.gist: GPT-3, released to little interest, learned to follow directions and solve tasks purely from prompts, implying its attention serves as fast weights that have learned to learn.

n0006.title: Meta-Learning
n0006.gist: One model to rule them all: 175b parameters solving arithmetic, translation, and analogies purely from prompted examples, with no finetuning.

n0008.title: Learning To Learn
n0008.gist: GPT-3's few-shot abilities suggest its attention mechanisms are fast weights that learned to learn from sufficiently varied data.

n0010.title: Flexing GPT
n0010.gist: GPT-3 is an obsolete architecture trained the dumbest way possible, yet it manifests runtime meta-learning with scaling curves still unbending—and standard NLP benchmarks miss all of it.

n0011.title: Dorian Gray Epigraph
n0011.gist: Wilde on brute reason: 'I can stand brute force, but brute reason is quite unbearable.'

n0014.title: Attacks Only Get Better
n0014.gist: GPT-3 is magnificently obsolete—a small, shallow, dumbly-trained model—and yet it shows crazy runtime meta-learning while the scaling curves still are not bending.

n0016.title: Benchmarks Miss The Leap
n0016.gist: Standard NLP benchmarks fail to capture GPT-3's flexible, creative generation; a post-GPT-3 task is benchmarking those capabilities, perhaps ARC-style.

n0018.title: Baking The Cake
n0018.gist: GPT-3 is not the whole picture but a big part: scaling is still working and predictably so, and the field's objections to further scaling are penny-wise, pound-foolish.

n0019.title: Is The Cake A Lie?
n0019.gist: GPT-3 doesn't set SOTA everywhere, but the question is whether it might work—and as an idiot savant of text, it looks like the unsupervised learning cake layers are finally rising.

n0024.title: Scaling Still Working
n0024.gist: GPT-3's scaling continues at roughly the same power-law past 100b parameters, strikingly predictable and suggesting trillions of parameters are both possible and useful.

n0027.title: Anti-Scaling: Penny-Wise, Pound-Foolish
n0027.gist: Researchers balk at GPT-3's cost, but further scaling of 100-1000× remains trivial by Big Science budgets, and it is easier to make something efficient after it exists.

n0029.title: Scaling
n0029.gist: The scaling laws hold for GPT-3 several orders past Kaplan et al 2020, leaving enormous room to run—and no way to predict what will emerge as loss keeps falling.

n0030.title: How Far Will Scaling Go?
n0030.gist: The scaling papers suggest the leaps so far are not even halfway in absolute loss, with clean power-law curves.

n0036.title: GPT-3 Keeps Scaling
n0036.gist: GPT-3's models continue obeying the scaling laws for several orders past Kaplan et al 2020, without the curve 'bouncing'.

n0039.title: What Emerges Next?
n0039.gist: With so much loss left to halve, nobody can predict what capabilities will emerge when—Bueller? Bueller?

n0041.title: Blessings Of Scale
n0041.gist: For deep learning, hard problems are easier than easy ones—everything improves with size—and this happens because big models are ensembles of sub-models whose Occam's-razor averaging, pushed by enough data, yields generalization and meta-learning.

n0042.title: Hard Problems Are Easier
n0042.gist: The blessings of scale: the bigger the net, compute, data, and problem, the better it learns—NNs are lazy and can do far more than we make them do.

n0047.title: Emergent Meta-Learning Everywhere
n0047.gist: Across domains—from AlphaZero to Dactyl to Procgen—simply training bigger models on harder, richer tasks induces generalization and meta-learning no one built in; as Botvinick says, you can't stop it.

n0050.title: Why Do They Generalize?
n0050.gist: Why do large models generalize better than small provably-equivalent ones, and what's up with double descent?

n0053.title: Ensembles And Occam's Razor
n0053.gist: Big models work because they encode countless sub-models which average out like an ensemble, biasing toward simple, flexible solutions.

n0055.title: Lazy Sub-Models, True Learning
n0055.gist: Memorizing sub-models learn quickest, but at Internet scale they can't memorize everything—so eventually the simplest model which predicts the data just is arithmetic, or meta-learning, and it's going to happen.

n0059.title: Scaling Hypothesis
n0059.gist: The strong scaling hypothesis—ever larger NNs on a scalable architecture will yield ever more sophisticated behavior—looked like numerology in 2004, but by 2020 its advocates had been vindicated.

n0060.title: The Strong Scaling Hypothesis
n0060.gist: Once we find a scalable architecture like self-attention, we can simply train ever larger NNs and ever more sophisticated behavior will emerge naturally, as brains are scaled-up primate brains.

n0063.title: I Was Wrong, They Were Right
n0063.gist: Skeptical of scaling advocates in 2004-6, the author concedes: we built the compute, and the algorithms did come.

n0065.title: Why Does Pretraining Work?
n0065.gist: Predicting text forces a model to progressively master everything from spelling to causality, because the last bits of loss require true understanding—and while the thesis once seemed like a magic trick, apparently it would've worked even with RNNs.

n0066.title: Humans Are The Cyanobacteria Of AI
n0066.gist: Human writings encode logic, causality, and history implicitly; a model learning to predict must learn to understand all of it, so solving the long tail means learning to generalize and reason.

n0071.title: From Letters To Sentences
n0071.gist: Training climbs from letter frequencies to vocabulary to word associations, until sentences start to make sense—each stage cheaper in bits than the last.

n0077.title: Errors Get Rarer, Not Easier
n0077.gist: As loss falls below ~2 bits, the remaining errors—pronouns, genre, coherence—become subtler and worth less than hundredths of a bit per character.

n0082.title: Everything It Misses
n0082.gist: The missing bits before human-level 0.7 require causality, commonsense, theory of mind, and logic—nothing less than true understanding suffices for ideal prediction.

n0086.title: The Last Bits Are Deepest
n0086.gist: Like human actions, everyday prediction is easy but the long tail of rare, consequential choices is where intelligence pays—explaining why those final bits demand the most.

n0091.title: Reasons For Doubt
n0091.gist: The pretraining thesis felt like a magic trick: it could require impossible data, broken architectures, or endless surface-level absorption—and yet apparently even RNNs would've worked.

n0096.title: Nobody Predicted It
n0096.gist: No one quantitatively predicted where GPT-3's capabilities emerged, and no one knows what another halving of the loss would gain.

n0103.title: Prospects
n0103.gist: The compute exists; what's missing is conviction—Google and DeepMind lack faith in the scaling hypothesis, while OpenAI bet the company on it, and so far no rival has even matched GPT-3.

n0104.title: The Missing Piece Is Conviction
n0104.gist: Knowing the answer exists changes everything, and as Sutskever says, the ideas were all there—what was missing was data, compute, and conviction.

n0109.title: Who Believes In Scaling?
n0109.gist: The hardware overhang means the limiting factor is human: will any organization treat GPT-3 as a Sputnik moment, or do Google Brain and DeepMind simply lack the vision?

n0112.title: DeepMind's Weak Scaling Hypothesis
n0112.gist: Google Brain is too short-term, while DeepMind believes AGI requires finding the right brain-like algorithms piece by piece—scalable, but needing invention and assembly.

n0115.title: Betting The Company On Scaling
n0115.gist: Others are uninterested, but OpenAI restructured into a for-profit subsidiary to fund its startup-like bet that the scaling hypothesis is true.

n0118.title: Lacking The Courage Of Convictions
n0118.gist: Competitors could replicate scaling with trivial budgets, but lack the courage of their convictions—and 152 days on, no model has even exceeded Turing-NLG's 17b.

n0121.title: Critiquing The Critics
n0121.gist: The DL revolution was easily predicted by a few connectionists like Moravec, the critics' dismissive 'voice of authority' is phatic rather than predictive, and reductionist 'just X' success is precisely what AI progress looks like.

n0122.title: Hindsight Is 20/20
n0122.gist: In 2010, deep learning believers fit in a conference room; a decade of Cambrian explosion vindicated Moravec's hardware forecasts, with 28 years of prediction left.

n0129.title: It Must Be 'Just X'
n0129.gist: Kasparov saw an alien intelligence in Deep Blue, and that dichotomy will grow—but reducing intelligence to 'just X' is precisely what success in AI must look like.

n0135.title: Authority Without Accountability
n0135.gist: Eminent experts projected failure routinely and were wrong, with few mea culpas—a puzzling failure worth reflecting on.

n0137.title: Phatic, Not Predictive
n0137.gist: The 'voice of authority' assures calm, makes no falsifiable predictions, and is never surprised—ask instead: what objective fact would change its mind?

n0143.title: It From Byte
n0143.gist: GPT-style models learn agency by imitating agents, and agency cannot be engineered away, because it is a convergent, useful capability that may emerge even from non-agentic data like physics.

n0144.title: Imitation Breeds Agency
n0144.gist: GPT-3 does offline imitation learning of agents, so prompting yields roleplayed planning and real-world action—and there is no principled definition of 'agent' that excludes these systems.

n0152.title: All Is Atoms & Void
n0152.gist: There is no hard line between agentic and non-agentic data, since all agency is made of non-agentic atoms—and even harmless data like river hydrology might evolve agency.

n0156.title: Intentional Interpretive Stance
n0156.gist: Via Dennett's intentional stance and the variational principle, treating systems as agents is a predictively useful shortcut a neural net will love—and even random Turing machines may induce theory of mind, so there is no escape from agency.

n0183.title: Ambient Agency
n0183.gist: Agency is like Turing-completeness: too useful and convergent to guarantee its absence, so abandon the idea that tool AIs cannot be agent AIs—tampering with data is not a solution.
